title: Describing with adjectives
topic: adjective agreement; position; muy and mucho
why: After ser and estar, you learn to describe: adjective agreement, position after the noun, the short forms buen, mal, gran, and the difference between muy and mucho. You can now describe your city, your neighborhood and your home before the unit review.

{"lessons": ["

Adjective agreement

In English, an adjective never changes: \"a pretty street, pretty streets\". In Spanish, the adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun, and you can always hear it, because the -a and the -s are pronounced.

Endingmasc. sing.fem. sing.masc. pl.fem. pl.
-o / -abonitobonitabonitosbonitas
-egrandegrandegrandesgrandes
consonantfácilfácilfácilesfáciles
-or / -oratrabajadortrabajadoratrabajadorestrabajadoras
nationalityespañolespañolaespañolesespañolas
  • Adjectives in -o make their feminine in -a: un barrio bonito, una calle bonita.
  • Adjectives in -e don't change in the feminine: un piso grande, una casa grande. Never \"granda\"!
  • Most adjectives ending in a consonant don't change either: un ejercicio fácil, una pregunta fácil. In the plural, they take -es: fáciles, jóvenes.
  • Adjectives in -or and nationalities add -a in the feminine: trabajadora, española.
Las calles son antiguas y los edificios son modernos.The streets are old and the buildings are modern.
Elena y Javier son trabajadores.Elena and Javier are hardworking.

A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Elena y Javier son simpáticos. And the adjective also agrees after ser and estar: La casa es bonita, Las chicas están cansadas.

", "

Where the adjective goes

In Spanish, the adjective almost always goes after the noun, the opposite of English:

un piso luminoso, una ciudad tranquila, un coche nuevoa bright apartment, a quiet city, a new car

Colors and nationalities always go after the noun: un coche rojo (a red car), una amiga francesa. Where English says \"a small apartment\", Spanish usually says un piso pequeño.

Buen, mal, gran: adjectives that get shorter

Three common adjectives often go before the noun. They then lose their ending:

Adjectivebefore a masculine singular nounbefore a feminine singular noun
buenoun buen libro (a good book)una buena idea (a good idea)
maloun mal día (a bad day)una mala noticia (bad news)
grandeun gran amigo (a great friend)una gran ciudad (a great city)
  • bueno and malo lose their -o only before a masculine singular noun: un buen día, but una buena idea, unos buenos amigos.
  • grande becomes gran before any singular noun, masculine or feminine: un gran amigo, una gran ciudad.
  • After the noun, they keep their full form: un día bueno, un piso grande.

A handy distinction: before the noun, gran means \"great, important\": un gran amigo (a great friend). After the noun, grande is about size: un piso grande (a big, spacious apartment).

", "

Muy or mucho?

English says \"very\" before an adjective and \"a lot (of)\", \"much\" or \"many\" before a noun or after a verb. Spanish makes the same distinction, with muy and mucho.

UseFormExamples
muy + adjective or adverbnever changesmuy bonito, muy bonitas, muy bien
mucho + nounagrees with the nounmucho tráfico, mucha gente, muchos bares, muchas tiendas
verb + muchonever changesTrabajo mucho. Leemos mucho.
Madrid es una ciudad muy bonita y tiene muchos museos.Madrid is a very beautiful city and it has a lot of museums.
En el centro vive mucha gente.A lot of people live downtown.
—¿Es caro el piso? —Sí, mucho.—Is the apartment expensive? —Yes, very.

Traps for an English speaker

  • No \"of\" after mucho: \"a lot of bars\" = muchos bares.
  • la gente is singular: mucha gente (a lot of people), and the verb stays singular.
  • Never \"muy\" before a noun, never \"mucho\" before an adjective: muy grande, mucho trabajo.
  • On its own as an answer, where English says \"Yes, very\", Spanish says mucho: —¿Es interesante? —Sí, mucho.

Describing your city and your home

To say that a place has something, you can use tener: El barrio tiene muchas tiendas. And to say where it is, estar: El piso está en el centro.

El piso es pequeño, pero muy luminoso. Está en una calle tranquila.The apartment is small, but very bright. It's on a quiet street.

Reminder: ser to describe (la calle es ruidosa), estar to locate or express a state (la calle está en el centro, estoy contento).
